paper_title: FlowEvo: Self-Evolving Agents through the Co-Evolution of Workflows and Executable Skills

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model agents can adapt to complex tasks by constructing workflows at inference time, but procedures discovered in one episode are usually discarded after execution. Existing skill libraries provide reusable executable routines, but are typically assembled offline and do not grow from the agent's own workflows. We introduce FlowEvo, a training-free framework in which workflows and skills co-evolve at inference time. FlowEvo compiles successful workflows into callable skills, stores them in a persistent bank, and uses retrieved skills either through direct execution or as context for constructing new workflows. It also tracks each skill's downstream utility and suppresses skills that cause negative transfer. Using a shared GPT-4o-mini backbone, FlowEvo achieves the highest accuracy among 8 baselines on the full standard splits of ALFWorld, HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, and MATH-500. On ALFWorld, it reaches 85.6%, 26.4 points above the strongest baseline, while using roughly one third as many tokens. Across 10 base models spanning 7B to 671B parameters, FlowEvo outperforms ExpeL in 49 of 50 model-dataset comparisons. Code is available at https://github.com/DEFENSE-SEU/FlowEvo.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly solve tasks by constructing workflows at inference time rather than following fixed prompt or fixed sequence of tool calls (Hu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025d). Solving task may involve decomposition, tool use, code generation, intermediate checking, and repair (Wang et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025a; Zheng et al., 2025b), and such agents are deployed across AI for science (Xu et al., 2026), from computational fluid dynamics (Yue et al., 2026c) and materials science (Zhu et al., 2026) to Earth observation (Yao et al., 2026) and automated scientific peer review (Wang et al., 2026a). This flexibility brings clear gains, but useful procedures discovered during one episode are rarely retained as skills: executable routines, with an interface and usage guidance, that later tasks can invoke (Zhao et al., 2024). Agents therefore repeatedly rediscover similar routines across related tasks, increasing token cost and variance (Sumers et al., 2023). The reusable operational structure inside successful workflow (Zhu et al., 2023), such as decomposition pattern or stable code scaffold, is discarded with the transient trajectory of the episode that produced it. Existing work addresses the two sides separately. One line stores prior plans, traces, or workflows as text and uses them to guide later generation (Wang et al., 2024b; Sarukkai et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026b; 2025c; Park et al., 2023); text record can describe what worked, but it cannot be invoked or validated, so reuse still depends on the model re-deriving the procedure. Another line treats tools, procedures, or skills as executable objects (Zheng et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023); such libraries are callable and Equal contribution. Corresponding authors: shimin.di@seu.edu.cn, pans2@rpi.edu. 1 Figure 1: Overview of FlowEvo. Successful workflows are compiled into executable skills and stored in persistent bank. Retrieved skills can either be executed directly or supplied as structured context for subsequent workflow generation. checkable, but they are typically constructed offline for fixed task distribution, apart from the agents own problem solving. Successful workflows lie between these two views. They contain more executable structure than text-based memory, but are less fixed than handdesigned tools. This raises basic question: when an agent solves tasks through workflows, how should successful workflows be turned into reusable skills, and how should those skills affect later workflow construction when model parameters remain fixed? We study this question with FlowEvo (Figure 1), training-free framework for self-evolving agents through the co-evolution of workflows and executable skills. When the agent solves task successfully, the useful part of the workflow is compiled into skill record and stored in persistent bank; retrieved records are executed directly on compatible tasks and otherwise supplied as structured context for new workflows (Section 3). This design creates workflowskillworkflow loop: execution produces successful traces, traces are compiled into executable skills, and the accumulated bank changes how later tasks are solved. The bank contributes in 2 ways: direct skill reuse, where validated callable artifact is executed on new task, and skill-conditioned workflow generation, where retrieved skills shape planning and generation without being replayed directly. Distinguishing the two matters because an improvement from skill accumulation should not be reduced to exact replay of previously stored solutions alone. Experiments cover the full standard splits of 5 benchmarks, spanning an interactive environment (ALFWorld; Shridhar et al., 2020) and code and math generation (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, MATH-500). FlowEvo attains the best accuracy on every benchmark against 8 classic and recent baselines, the advantage holds across 10 base models, and controlled ablations attribute it to each mechanism (Section 4). Our contributions are as follows: Workflow-to-skill compilation: an online compilation step that turns successful workflows into reusable skill records combining callable artifact with structured guidance. Tiered skill-to-workflow reuse: routing mechanism over dynamic generation, direct skill execution, and skill-conditioned workflow generation, with direct execution falling back to conditioning when preconditions or validation fail. Contrastive-utility lifecycle: lifecycle that tracks each skills downstream utility and automatically suppresses skills exhibiting persistently negative transfer.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Workflow generation and optimization. growing line of work constructs workflows dynamically at inference time (Yue et al., 2026a; Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Khattab et al., 2 2023; Zhu et al., 2025). Some methods search directly over workflow structure or optimize workflow graphs offline, from agent societies as optimizable graphs (Zhuge et al., 2024) and meta-agent search (Hu et al., 2024) to MCTS-based optimization (Zhang et al., 2025b) and agentic supernets (Zhang et al., 2025a); recent systems add safety-constrained evolutionary programming (Zheng et al., 2025b), evolving multi-agent platforms (Wang et al., 2025c), dynamic designerexecutor workflows (Wang et al., 2025b), and deterministic routing orchestrators (Zhou & Chan, 2026). We include these 4 systems, together with ADAS and AFlow, as baselines. The approaches above establish the importance of workflow structure but optimize for the current task or benchmark. We instead ask how successful workflows become reusable artifacts that remain available after the original task has finished. Memory for workflow agents. Another line augments agents with memories of prior plans, traces, or routines (Zhang et al., 2025d; Xu et al., 2025b). Agent Workflow Memory (Wang et al., 2024b) is the closest in spirit, storing workflow-level experience to guide later generation, and Sarukkai et al. (2025) show that even naively accumulated self-generated trajectories improve sequential decision-making as in-context examples. Text-based memories improve planning, but they describe prior behavior rather than provide directly executable procedures. That gap motivates converting successful workflows into skill records that combine callable artifacts with structured guidance (Wang et al., 2025a; Xia et al., 2026b). Skills, tools, and executable reuse. separate literature treats reusable procedures, tools, APIs, and skills as first-class objects that are more verifiable and reusable than text-only memories (Cai et al., 2023; Qian et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Zheng et al., 2025a; Ouyang et al., 2026; Di et al., 2026). However, these methods typically construct tools for fixed task distribution (Yuan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a) or decouple tool creation from the agents own problem-solving trajectory (Qian et al., 2023; Cai et al., 2023; Xia et al., 2026a). Recent skill-centric systems organize large pre-built corpora offline (Liang et al., 2026), evolve skills across multi-user population (Ma et al., 2026), or fine-tune weights alongside the library (Xia et al., 2026c). FlowEvo differs on both axes. Its skills are compiled online from the agents own verifier-passed traces, and the update is training-free. Training-free adaptation and self-evolution. Recent work explores how agents improve over time without weight updates, using search, self-generated feedback, memory revision, or evolving control state (Madaan et al., 2023; Putta et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026a;b; Tian et al., 2024; Yue et al., 2025). This line has early roots in late-20232024 systems that improve an agents prompts, scaffolds, or collective topology at inference time. Promptbreeder (Fernando et al., 2023) evolves prompt populations self-referentially, STOP (Zelikman et al., 2024) recursively rewrites the scaffolding program that invokes the model, and GPTSwarm (Zhuge et al., 2024) optimizes the communication graph of an agent society. In interactive environments, CLIN (Majumder et al., 2024) maintains continually revised memory of causal abstractions. Closest to our setting, Evoflux (Bhandari et al., 2026) evolves executable tool workflows at inference time for compact agents. FlowEvo shares the training-free premise of this lineage, but the evolving object is more operationally grounded, namely an executable skill bank distilled from the agents own successful workflows and governed by explicit admission and curation policies. Position of this work. Across these lines, one problem remains unresolved: how workflowbased agent can persistently accumulate reusable capability from its own successful executions. Workflow optimization rarely preserves what was learned in executable form, text memory cannot be verified or invoked, tool creation happens outside the agents own online loop, and self-evolution methods lack concrete accumulation mechanism. FlowEvo addresses this gap by compiling successful workflows into reusable skill records and feeding them back through direct reuse and skill-conditioned workflow generation.

sections.title: 3.1 Problem setup and the workflow-to-skill-to-workflow loop
sections.content: Consider stream of tasks {xt}T t=1. At episode t, the agent operates with an inferencetime context Ct = (Bt, Mt, Rt), where Bt is the executable skill bank, Mt denotes auxiliary 3 memory layers, and Rt collects the retrieval, routing, and failure state accumulated from prior use. Given task xt, FlowEvo retrieves candidate artifacts, selects routing mode, constructs workflow plan Wt when needed, executes and verifies the resulting program to obtain trace τt and outcome yt, and, when successful episode yields reusable structure, compiles candidate executable artifact and updates the memory state: Wt = G(xt; Ct), (τt, yt) = E(xt, Wt), (Bt+1, Mt+1, Rt+1) = U(Bt, Mt, Rt, τt, yt). Self-evolution therefore occurs through updates to executable and non-executable memory, with the base model held fixed throughout the stream. (1) The central design choice is that successful workflows are compiled into executable skills rather than retained as text. retrieved skill may be executed directly when compatibility and validation make reuse reliable enough, or exposed only as structured context guiding the generation of new workflow. The skill bank is thus persistent inference-time capability layer rather than prompt text alone. Algorithm 1 in Appendix presents the complete per-episode procedure in pseudocode with inline comments. System decomposition. Operationally, FlowEvo consists of 4 tightly coupled components: workflow planner, an executor with verification, trace-to-skill compiler, and skill registry with lifecycle curation. The compiler extracts reusable executable artifacts only from verifierpassed successful episodes, while the registry maintains retrieval indices, admission state, and lifecycle updates. This decomposition makes the loop directly observable at the trace level and helps attribute downstream gains to specific stored skills rather than to untracked prompt history in the context window of the base model.

sections.title: 3.2 Skill representation
sections.content: A skill record in FlowEvo is structured artifact that pairs an executable component with auxiliary textual guidance, rather than free-form text note. The executable component is subject to interface, replay, and safety checks at admission where feasible, while the textual guidance supports skill-conditioned generation when direct execution is not selected. At high level, each skill is = ( , σ, , m, ℓ), where is the executable body with an identified entry point, σ an explicit callable interface, set of replay or verifier tests, associated metadata, and ℓ the current lifecycle state of the record. The metadata makes skill reuse explicit and auditable in practice. It records provenance (source task and fold), task-pattern tags, direct-reuse eligibility, preferred usage mode, reuse and fallback constraints, lightweight routing statistics, and negative evidence used to downweight previously harmful skills. Not all fields are exposed in every route, but together they allow retrieved skill to be called through known interface, checked against stored validation data, and systematically tracked as its downstream behavior changes across later episodes of the stream that reuse or audit the skill. The same stored artifact supports both reuse modes: direct execution relies on the interface, preconditions, eligibility for direct use, and replay evidence, while skill-conditioned generation exposes compact structured view of the same artifact (signature, task pattern, scaffold hint, or short code excerpt). The two uses have different reliability requirements and are therefore evaluated separately in the mechanism analyses.

sections.title: 3.3 Workflow generation with retrieved skill context
sections.content: For each task, retriever scores candidate skills using lexical overlap, task-pattern compatibility, interface compatibility, and historical utility signals. The retriever is also aware of negative evidence, so previously harmful or mismatched skills are penalized rather than treated as fresh candidates at the next retrieval. For clarity, we group the planners behavior into 3 main routes: (i) dynamic generation with no retrieved skill, (ii) direct execution of retrieved skill, and (iii) skill-conditioned generation in which retrieved skills are supplied only as structured context (Table 13, Appendix C). Inside the third branch, the implementation contains finer-grained seeded modes. The distinction between routes (ii) and (iii) is central to the mechanism analysis. 4 Direct execution is permitted only for skills that remain compatible after filtering and validation. Skill-conditioned generation is used when retrieval is informative enough to guide planning but not reliable enough for direct execution, or when direct execution is intentionally disabled for analysis. The planner then injects compact structured view of the skill rather than replaying the full artifact, which limits prompt overhead and makes gains attributable to structured reuse rather than unrestricted replay.

sections.title: 3.4 Compiling successful workflows into executable skills
sections.content: When task succeeds, FlowEvo compiles the verified trace into reusable executable artifact rather than textual summary. The compiler identifies an entry point, infers callable signature, extracts replay tests when possible, and records source and task-pattern tags together with metadata used for routing, such as reuse constraints and preferred usage mode. Compilation is attempted only from verifier-passed successful episodes, and the emitted candidate is passed to the admission layer, which may retain it for direct execution, retain it only for context exposure, or leave it in shadow state for diagnostics. The result is callable artifact that can be replayed, retrieved, and validated on later tasks in the stream.

sections.title: 3.5 Admission and skill curation
sections.content: Not every successful trace should enter the active bank directly. Each candidate skill is first checked for duplicates and then passed through an admission layer governed by 3 diagnostic dimensions: interface compliance, whether the extracted skill can be called under the intended signature and preconditions; functional correctness, whether replay tests and held-out checks support the claimed behavior; and safety compliance, whether the skill respects deployment constraints such as banned imports and banned calls (Appendix E). Skills that fail these checks are not exposed for direct execution; borderline cases may be retained only for skill-conditioned use or shadowed for diagnosis. Once admitted, skills remain subject to lifecycle control based on their downstream utility: whether the skill improves later solving rather than merely existing in the bank. FlowEvo tracks utility, failure patterns, and audit outcomes, and can disable, restrict, repair, or prune skill when repeated negative transfer accumulates. Current policies are conservative, re-checking suspicious skills with targeted audit episodes and downgrading direct-use privileges before removal. Unlike the admission dimensions, downstream utility cannot be evaluated at admission time and is assessed continuously after the skill enters the bank. key mechanism for detecting negative transfer is contrastive evaluation: for each actively used skill, FlowEvo periodically compares the success rate of episodes where the skill was applied against matched episodes where it was withheld, and flags the skill for suppression when this contrastive delta is persistently negative. This provides lightweight causal signal for identifying harmful skills without explicit holdout experiments or ground-truth labels for individual skill contributions. The signal complements causal failure attribution in broader multi-agent systems (Ma et al., 2025).

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We first compare FlowEvo with the 8 baselines on the full standard splits of the 5 benchmarks to demonstrate its accuracy and cost advantage (Section 4.2). We then vary the backbone across 10 base models to show that the advantage does not depend on single model (Section 4.3). Finally, we isolate each mechanism through controlled ablations on ALFWorld, with further analyses of weak-supervision robustness, bank scalability, and accumulation dynamics (Sections 4.4 and 4.5); complementary fixed-bank mechanism analyses on MBPP are reported in Appendix together with the protocol details.

sections.title: 4.4 Ablation study: 3 mechanisms
sections.content: Table 4 isolates each mechanism through controlled ablations against ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), which uses interleaved reasoning and acting without skill accumulation. Switching on one mechanism at time contributes +5.2 points for compilation, +41.8 for skill-toworkflow feedback, and +5.0 for curation. Compilation without reuse already helps because extracting reusable structure from successful trajectories regularizes behavior, improving auxiliary memories and intermediate representations. Skill-to-workflow feedback. Enabling skill reuse on top of compilation produces the dominant improvement (38.8% to 80.6%), confirming that the gain is driven by skill feedback rather than curation. Compiled skills are retrieved and either executed directly or injected as structured context. On ALFWorld, where task types recur with parametric variation, direct reuse dominates the routing mix (Section 4.5). 8 (a) Token cost per episode (b) Cumulative reuse and hit rate Figure 2: Skill accumulation dynamics on ALFWorld (representative run). (a) Token cost drops sharply once the first skill reuse occurs around episode 10 (dashed line) and stays at or below ReAct. (b) Cumulative direct-reuse count (blue, solid) grows nearly linearly to 101/134; the reuse hit rate (orange, dashed) stabilizes around 75%. Skill curation. Curation contributes +5.0 points and qualitatively important safeguard against negative transfer. In one seed of the 3-seed campaign, contrastive evaluation identified the pick_two_obj_and_place skill as harmful: guided success was 2/14 (14%) versus 1/3 (33%) unguided, delta of 0.19, below the suppression threshold of 0.1, triggering suppression within 14 guided episodes (Appendices and G). Without curation this skill would keep harming subsequent episodes. With curation, routing for this task type defaults to dynamic generation. Skill accumulation is thus not uniformly beneficial, and curation keeps the bank from amplifying its own worst entries. Robustness to weak or noisy supervision. Compilation is gated on verifier-passed traces, so one may worry that FlowEvo requires clean success signals. 3-condition ablation of the admission gate (3 seeds; Table 10) shows otherwise: removing the trace-success requirement costs 1.5 points (85.6% 84.1%), and flipping 20% of pass/fail labels in both directions costs 1.7 points. Neither change is significant under McNemars test (p > 0.1). The 2-stage design, which pairs verifier pass at compile time with contrastive checking during use, absorbs upstream label noise without extra supervision. Skill-bank scalability. Across the 134 episodes the bank saturates at 7 workflow templates (one per task type plus one blueprint entry) and 18 exemplars. The first 28 episodes cover 5 task types, and the rest add single entry (Tables 11 and 12). De-duplication and contrastive suppression keep the bank compact and retrieval cost bounded.

sections.title: 4.5 Analysis of skill accumulation dynamics
sections.content: Token efficiency and reuse. Figure 2 plots the representative run of Appendices FG. After the first skill reuse occurs (around episode 10), token consumption drops sharply and stays low, because direct reuse bypasses exploratory interaction. Averaged over 3 seeds, FlowEvo uses 9,329 tokens per episode against 29,67132,958 for the baselines. The cumulative directreuse count grows steadily to 101 of 134 episodes, the hit rate stabilizes around 75%, and 99 of the 101 direct-reuse episodes succeed (98%). Per-task-type improvement. Decomposing the success rate by task type in Figure 3 and Appendix shows that the improvement tracks the direct-hit rate, that is, how often the compiled skill completed the task through direct execution alone. Gains fall from +78 points at direct-hit rate of 83% on pick_heat_then_place_in_recep to +28 points at 0% on look_at_obj_in_light. The latter isolates the second reuse mode: the skill matched on 15 of 18 episodes but completed none through direct execution (Tables 1516). The sixth type, pick_two_obj_and_place, was suppressed by curation (Section 4.4). Fixed-bank mechanism analyses on MBPP. Appendix isolates the two reuse modes under growth-to-frozen MBPP protocol. On exact-transfer cases, executable reuse beats dynamic generation on both accuracy and cost (85.9% at 204 tokens vs. 81.7% at 224), while text workflow memory trades +1.4 points for 85% more tokens. On the full evaluation split, no router pair separates under paired testing (all pairwise McNemar > 0.5).

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Accumulated skills help through 2 complementary mechanisms. The dominant one is direct skill reuse. On ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020), compiled skills are replayed on the majority of episodes at 98% success rate in the representative run, consistent with the +41.8-point skill-feedback gain over 3 seeds. The second is skill-conditioned generation when direct replay is unavailable. This mode is the relevant one on code and math, isolated by the look_at_obj_in_light case and the fixed-bank MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) analyses (Appendix A), which freeze the bank before evaluation. FlowEvo also clarifies the relation between workflow optimization and skill learning, preserving the stable parts of successful workflow as persistent executable object with an interface, validation tests, and usage history. The comparison with text memory is not onesided: on the MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) exact-transfer slice, text workflow memory attains slightly higher pass rate at much higher cost. At comparable accuracy, however, executable skills give better accuracyefficiency frontier, together with verifiability, invocability, and auditability that text record, however detailed, cannot provide. The backbone sweep indicates where an inference-time capability layer matters most. Across 10 base models the gain over ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) is positive in 49 of 50 modeldataset cells, and within the GPT-4.1 ladder it widens as model size decreases, reaching +53.2 points on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2020) for the smallest model while HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) sit near saturation. The ladder holds family and generation fixed, so the widening gap tracks scale rather than family idiosyncrasy, and the breadth panel repeats the direction across dense and mixture-of-experts designs, with mean gain of +11.0 points and median of +7.0 over the full 50 cells. Median and mean agree in sign, so the improvement is broad rather than concentrated in few cells. The pattern is consistent with compiled skills supplying structure that stronger backbone can reconstruct on demand. The largest gains therefore fall where the base model is weakest, which is also where inference is least expensive. The single trailing cell, Qwen3-8B on MATH500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), marks the lower end of that range, where too few candidate skills survive admission to populate the bank and support retrieval. Above that floor the loop engages without further requirements on the backbone, and the advantage narrows only where the base model alone already sits near ceiling accuracy, as on HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021). The capability layer is thus complementary to scale: it substitutes structure where the backbone lacks it and steps aside where the backbone can already reconstruct that structure on demand. The current evidence should guide interpretation. Our experiments rely on domains where correctness can be checked with environment feedback or hidden tests. The ALFWorld results and the admission-gate ablation show that the loop tolerates weak and even noisy signals. Fully signal-free settings such as free-form dialogue and long-form writing remain out of scope, and delayed, partial, or adversarial feedback may pose further challenges (Wang et al., 2026a). The framework also needs enough base capability to bootstrap the loop (see the Qwen3-8B MATH-500 cell in Table 3). There are 2 directions. First, self-evolution could extend beyond task-solving skills to the rest of the agent harness (Guo et al., 2026), including verification helpers, retry policies, and retrieval heuristics, and to broader tool ecosystems via standardized protocols (Ouyang et al., 2026; Di et al., 2026). Second, bank maintenance under long-running use is problem in its own right, requiring skills to be revised, merged, and retired while limiting retrieval interference (Yue et al., 2026b; Guo et al., 2025).

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: FlowEvo compiles successful workflows into reusable skill records for direct execution or structured context. Across 5 full-split benchmarks, it achieves the highest accuracy among 8 baselines and Pareto-dominates ADAS (Hu et al., 2024) and AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025b) on 4 of 5. Gains persist across 10 base models; ablations identify skill feedback as the main contributor. Agents can improve at inference time by retaining reusable execution structure.

In Forty-first International Conference on Machine Learning, 2024. 15 Fixed-Bank Mechanism Analyses on MBPP The main-text ALFWorld analyses study skill accumulation online, as the bank grows. This appendix isolates the two reuse modes under frozen bank, so that downstream effects are attributable to previously accumulated capabilities rather than to continued adaptation. Fixed-bank protocol. The MBPP mechanism analyses use deterministic 3-fold growthto-frozen protocol over fixed task universe. In each fold, one partition is used during growth phase to accumulate skills and workflow memories, while the held-out partition is reserved for fixed-bank evaluation. During growth, FlowEvo may compile new skills, summarize workflows, and revise routing statistics. During the subsequent fixed-bank phase, all such updates are disabled: no new skills are compiled, no routing statistics are revised, and no additional workflow memories are added. We study 2 held-out settings on this MBPP universe. Exact-transfer evaluation aggregates 71 held-out cases that admit direct execution of compatible previously acquired skill. Compatible non-exact evaluation uses 44 held-out tasks that do not admit exact replay but do admit transfer from related acquired skill through structured context; each such task is evaluated over 3 fresh task orders, yielding 132 fixed-bank episodes in total. A.1 Exact-transfer analysis: executable skills as efficient direct reuse Table 5 evaluates held-out cases in which compatible previously acquired skill can be executed directly. Under this protocol, FlowEvo selects the direct-execution route on all 71 cases. Relative to dynamic generation, executable reuse improves pass rate from 81.7% to 85.9% while reducing average token usage from 224.2 to 204.4. Text workflow memory attains slightly higher pass rate at 87.3%, but does so at substantially greater cost: it leads executable reuse by 1.4 points while using 85% more tokens. sections.title: E Framework Thresholds and Configuration Constants
sections.content: FlowEvos routing, admission, and curation decisions are governed by set of numeric thresholds. Table 14 lists the values that affect the results reported in Section 4. The full set of 177 constants appears in the released code. The contrastive harm threshold 0.1, combined with the minimum-samples gates (_CONTRASTIVE_MIN_GUIDED = 5, _CONTRASTIVE_MIN_UNGUIDED = 3), determines when skill curation suppresses skill: candidate is suppressed only after at least 5 guided and 3 unguided samples, and only if the delta falls below 0.1. The suppression event reported in Section 4.4 (guided 2/14, unguided 1/3, = 0.19) satisfies these gates: 14 5, 3 3, and 0.143 0.333 = 0.19 < 0.1. The analogous event in the representative run of Appendix (guided 1/10 vs. unguided 1/3, = 0.23) satisfies them as well: 10 5, 3 3, and 0.1 0.333 = 0.233 < 0.1, so the suppression trigger fires in both runs.
